title: Association between daily alcohol intake and risk of all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analyses
authors: Zhao J, Stockwell T, Naimi T, Churchill S, Clay J, Sherk A
population: 107 cohort studies published 1980 to July 2021, 425,564 deaths
funder: This study was partly funded by the CCSA as a subcontract for a Health Canada grant to develop guidance for Canadians on alcohol and health. Health Canada had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; and decision to submit the manuscript for publication. CCSA staff conducted a preliminary search to identify potentially relevant articles but did not participate in decisions about inclusion/exclusion of studies, coding, analysis, interpretation of results or approving the final manuscript.
authorConflicts: Stockwell reported personal fees from the Ontario Public Servants Employees Union for expert witness testimony and personal fees from Alko outside the submitted work; Sherk reported grants from the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA) during the study.
result: 21 of 107 studies were free of abstainer bias. Low-volume drinkers (1.3 to 24.0 g per day) had RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.88) unadjusted, against abstainers as defined in the included studies, and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) against lifetime non-drinkers after full adjustment for abstainer biases and study characteristics; fully adjusted, occasional drinkers 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06); 25 to 44 g per day 1.05 (0.96 to 1.14); 45 to 64 g per day 1.19 (1.07 to 1.32); 65 g per day or more 1.35 (1.23 to 1.47). Women drinking 25 to 44 g per day had RR 1.21 (1.08 to 1.36).
